subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 19-year-old man is brought in after eating berries from a plant he found while hiking. He is agitated and incoherent. Examination shows dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, and a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?
explanation_correct: This is the anticholinergic toxidrome (hot, dry, mad, blind, full). Physostigmine is a tertiary amine that crosses the blood-brain barrier and reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase centrally and peripherally. Supportive cooling is also required; physostigmine is avoided when tricyclic antidepressant co-ingestion is suspected.

explanation_incorrect.B: Neostigmine is a quaternary amine that does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it cannot reverse central anticholinergic effects.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atropine is itself a muscarinic antagonist and would worsen the toxidrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pralidoxime is used for organophosphate poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase.
explanation_incorrect.E: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and has no role in anticholinergic toxicity.

educationalObjective: Physostigmine, a CNS-penetrant cholinesterase inhibitor, is the antidote for central anticholinergic toxicity.
